Histor is built on TLSNotary, an open-source protocol for proving what a TLS server sent. The verifier trusts two things: the witness’s public key, and the same public certificate authorities your browser trusts. 01 ### Connect The agent opens an ordinary TLS session to any HTTPS server: a weather feed, an FX rate API, a bank. Nothing is installed on that server. 02 ### Split the keys The Histor witness joins the session through multi-party computation (MPC-TLS). It holds half the session keys. The operator never holds the whole key, and the witness only ever sees ciphertext. 03 ### Co-sign The witness signs a commitment to the exact bytes that crossed the wire, with a session time it checks against its own clock to within 5 seconds. 04 ### Verify offline Anyone checks the receipt in about 10 ms with no network call. The agent can disclose single fields, such as one exchange rate, and keep the rest of the response hidden. MPC mode The witness holds half the TLS keys and never sees plaintext. temperature 27 °C · wind 12.96 km/h exit 0 Trimmed from the run log, not edited. TLSNotary v0.1.0-alpha.15, MPC-TLS, TLS 1.2. ### Two-agent payment demo 1 paid · 4 refused Agent A quotes the USD→EUR rate from api.frankfurter.dev (ECB reference rates). Agent B pays a €10,000 invoice in dollars at that rate. Every message between them passes through a relay that tries to cheat. Agent B acts only on a value inside a valid receipt, from the right server, for the right request, less than ten minutes old. Round | The relay | Agent B --- | --- | --- 1 | Forwards the message unchanged | Computes the payment at the witnessed rate 2 | Changes the rate, leaves the receipt | Refuses: the claim does not match the receipt 3 | Changes the rate and edits the receipt to match | Refuses: the receipt fails verification 4 | Swaps in a genuine receipt for USD→GBP | Refuses: the receipt answers a different request 5 | Strips the receipt | Refuses: unwitnessed claim The agents are scripted MCP clients, not language models, so runs repeat exactly. No money moved; agent B computes the payment. ~10 ms to verify a receipt, offline 2.8–4.0 s per witnessed call, MPC mode 27× less traffic in proxy mode 0 software installed on the server Measured on one machine with the witness running locally. A remote witness has not been measured yet. Limits ## What a receipt does not prove. A receipt proves what a named server sent, and when. Read it as exactly that. It does not prove * That the server told the truth. A receipt shows what api.weather.gov said, not the weather. * Anything about a server the operator controls. That receipt is still the operator’s word, now fixed in time and bytes. * That the agent sent every action through the witness. That takes credential custody or egress control. * Independence, when one party runs both the agent side and the witness. High-value receipts should carry more than one witness. * That the content is safe to act on. A genuine page can still carry a prompt injection. Engine limits today: TLS 1.2 only (TLS 1.3 is on TLSNotary’s roadmap), pre-release software, and no compressed or streamed responses. ## Two tools your agent already knows how to call. Histor ships as a CLI and an MCP server, so it works in Claude Code, Cursor and any MCP client. Receipts are content-addressed: agents pass a short receipt_id instead of 15 KB of base64. witnessed_fetch(url, fields?, mode?) GETs an https:// URL through a Histor witness. Returns the server, time, request and disclosed fields, plus a receipt_id. verify_receipt(receipt_id | receipt, expect_server?) Checks a receipt another agent handed you, offline. Returns what it proves, or the reason it fails. witnessed_request(url, method, body, request_fields?) POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE. Credentials for the target live on the server, so the model never sees a secret. The request body is committed and stays hidden unless you disclose named fields. The CLI and MCP server are released to pilot teams first. Request beta access For insurers and MGAs ## Underwrite from evidence the insured didn’t write. New AI-liability covers ask for agent logs, and today those logs are self-reported. Cyber insurers learned to price from external scans the insured couldn’t edit. A Histor receipt gives an AI-liability book the same kind of signal for agent actions. ### At claim time Check what the agent was told before it acted. The claims desk verifies the receipt itself, offline. ### At underwriting Witnessed actions as a share of all agent actions is a number the insured can’t inflate. ### Narrow by design A receipt proves what a named server sent and when. It makes no claim about whether the agent acted well. Never a value from anyone else. ## What a label does not say The profile HISTOR implements forbids the words safe, secure, audited, certified, approved and trusted. Here is why, in the terms of what the log can and cannot show. ### Not a safety rating A pattern match is a reason to read a definition, not a finding. Three of the four methods can never return fail. There is no score to rank by, because no score HISTOR could compute would mean what a reader takes it to mean. ### Not the code Labels are about advertised text. A remote endpoint's source is never read and its tools are never invoked; a package runs only in the sandbox, against nothing real. A server can keep identical definitions and behave differently for real users; the log cannot see that, and says so inside every label. ### A change is not an accusation A version bump changes definitions too. A change is shown as a date and a diff, in amber, never red. What you do with it is yours: re-read, re-approve, or pin the old digest. ### A package as run here, not on your machine An npm or PyPI server is observed under the test conditions above: Linux, no internet, placeholder keys. One that needs Windows, a real account or the network may show fewer tools or none; its page says why it exited. ### One operator, one key Today one party runs the log. A second observer on another network is the next step, and any AIMarket hub can run one. Until then, what the key proves is who said it — not that it is true. ### Behind a login, unseen Endpoints that require authentication answer 401 to everyone without a key, including HISTOR. They are counted and listed as not observed, never dropped from the numbers. No. The server list is the log's index: every remote endpoint in the official MCP registry, with what HISTOR could observe about it. Nothing here is for sale and nothing is ranked by quality. Does HISTOR tell me a server is safe? No, and it never will. It tells you what a server advertised, whether that changed, and which published patterns matched the text. Whether to trust the server is your decision — HISTOR makes sure you decide on the same facts as everyone else. Why are so many servers "not observed"? Most remote MCP endpoints require a login (they answer 401 to anyone without a key), some use the legacy SSE transport or need per-user values in the URL, and some are simply down. They stay on the list with the reason, so the numbers never hide them. How do I check a server I already use? Open the Check tab, paste the server's endpoint and the tools/list result your client received, and press Check.
